title: Complex differentiability
section: Complex Variables ▷ The Derivative of a Function of a Complex Variable

question.text:
Suppose f is complex differentiable at a and define F(z) = f(z) near a. Which formula is
valid?
′ ′
(A) F (a) = f (a)
′
′
(B) F (a) = −f (a)
′
′
(C) F (a) = f (a)
(D) F cannot be complex differentiable unless f is constant.
′
′
(E) F (a) = f (a)

solution.text:
The difference quotient of F is the conjugate of [f (a + h) − f(a)]/h. As h → 0, also
h → 0 through every direction. Taking the conjugate of the limit proves the formula. Con-
jugating both the input and the output is different from conjugating just one.

Define f(0) = 0 and f (z) = z /z for z ̸= 0. Which statement about f at zero is correct?
(A) It has no real partial derivatives.
(B) It is complex differentiable with derivative −1.
(C) It is discontinuous.
(D) It is continuous and has both real partial derivatives, but is not complex differentiable.
(E) It is complex differentiable with derivative 1.

solution.text:
Since |f(z)| = |z|, it is continuous at zero. Along the real axis f(t) = t, and along the imag-
inary axis f(it) = it, so the partial derivatives even satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations
2
at zero. But f (z)/z = (z/z) equals 1 on the real axis and −1 on the line z = t(1 + i), so no
complex derivative exists.

If f(z) = z + z, what is the set of points at which f is complex differentiable?
(A) The real axis (B) The empty set (C) The imaginary axis (D) {0} (E) All of C

solution.text:
2
The polynomial z is complex differentiable everywhere. If their sum were differentiable
2
at any point, subtracting z would make z differentiable there, but its difference quotients
along real and imaginary increments are 1 and −1.
